overview:
Germany's first experiment with parliamentary democracy was born out of defeat. In November 1918, with the army broken and sailors and workers in revolt, the Kaiser abdicated and a republic was proclaimed in Berlin on 9 November. A national assembly met the following year in the quiet town of Weimar, away from the street fighting in the capital, and produced a constitution that took effect in August 1919. It was strikingly modern for its day: a directly elected president in place of a hereditary emperor, votes for women, a voting age of twenty, and a Reichstag chosen by proportional representation. It also contained Article 48, which let the president suspend civil rights and rule by emergency decree — a clause meant for crises that would later be used to hollow the system out from within.

The republic's first years were violent and financially catastrophic. Left-wing risings and right-wing putsch attempts followed one another; hundreds died in Berlin street fighting in early 1919, political assassinations claimed government ministers, and Hitler's Beer Hall Putsch in Munich in 1923 was only one episode among many. Reparations under the Treaty of Versailles, war debts and a government that met them by printing money produced hyperinflation so extreme that the mark fell from roughly sixty-five to the dollar in January 1920 to some four trillion by November 1923; the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr and the passive resistance the government paid for made it worse. Stabilization came with a new currency and, from 1924, American loans under the Dawes Plan. The years that followed — sometimes called the golden twenties — brought booming industry, a growing welfare state, and the cultural explosion associated with Weimar: Bauhaus design, new cinema, cabaret, mass media and a remarkable openness about sex and the body. That flowering was concentrated in Berlin and a few large cities; nearly half of Germans still lived in communities of fewer than five thousand people, where older religious and rural patterns held.

The prosperity rested on foreign credit, and the Wall Street crash of 1929 pulled it away. Unemployment surged, coalition government broke down in 1930, and from then on chancellors — Brüning, then Papen, then Schleicher — governed largely by presidential decree under the aged Field Marshal Hindenburg rather than by Reichstag majority. Elections in 1930 and 1932 turned the Nazis and the Communists into the two largest blocs, leaving no workable parliamentary centre. On 30 January 1933 a circle of conservatives who believed they could contain him persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor. Within months the emergency powers written into the constitution had been used to dismantle it.
significance: Weimar became the standing case study in how a democracy can be destroyed by legal means, and its wreckage shaped what came after: the postwar Federal Republic deliberately weakened the presidency, imposed a five-percent electoral threshold to block splinter parties, and made basic rights unamendable, all as answers to specific Weimar failures. Its constitutional debates over emergency powers, proportional representation and the vulnerability of a republic without enough convinced republicans are still cited whenever democracies come under strain. At the same time the republic's own creations outlasted it — modern social insurance and urban planning, Bauhaus architecture and design, a body of film and literature, and an early movement for sexual and reproductive rights — much of it carried abroad after 1933 by the people the Nazis drove out.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all beneath the story, so the overview is written entirely from reference works — the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Britannica, Wikipedia and the German History in Documents introduction — and the map can show nothing for it. The surviving record for Weimar is unusually rich (elections, press, film, official papers), but it is read through the knowledge of what followed; historians now stress that the collapse was contingent rather than doomed, and that older accounts overweighted Berlin's cultural glitter while underdocumenting small-town and rural Germany, where most people actually lived.
